source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay
finding: Each possible memory backup gets priority EVB = Need x Gain. Gain is the policy improvement a backup would give. Need is the expected discounted future visits to that state, from the successor representation. Highest EVB is replayed first.
numbers: Eq. 5 gain = sum_a (pi_new - pi_old) q_new. Eq. 6 need = (I - gamma T)^-1. Sims: 50 episodes, 20 planning steps at episode start and end, gamma 0.9, softmax beta 5, 6x9 open field and two 1x10 linear tracks. Diba and Buzsaki 2007 data cited: 841 of 887 forward sequences before the run, 395 of 464 reverse sequences after the run.
quote: EVB(s_k, a_k) = Need(s_k) x Gain(s_k, a_k)
limits: Only simple stationary deterministic spatial tasks. No uncertainty. Myopic utility per backup. Gain needs knowing a backup's effect before doing it (authors call this unrealistic). Not a process model. No numeric effect size for the speed-up over random replay.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete rule for which stored subgoals to revisit: score = how much re-examining would change our plan (gain) times how likely the subgoal is to be needed again (need).

source: Mattar and Daw (2018), forward vs reverse replay result
finding: Forward replay appears before a move, when need dominates. Reverse replay appears after reward, when gain dominates. Need must be above zero for either pattern. Replay count falls with experience and peaks in novel settings.
numbers: Significant replay event = run of 5 or more consecutive forward or reverse backups, permutation test. Replay probability decays across episodes; gain falls with exposure while need rises as paths become predictable.
limits: Same simulation limits as above. The ordering claim is model output, not new human data.
agent_relevance: Two modes for our agent: before acting, order subgoals by likely need; right after a surprising success or failure, replay backward along the chain that led to it.

source: Liu, Mattar, Behrens, Daw, Dolan (2021) Experience replay is associated with efficient non-local learning, Science
finding: First human MEG test of the utility rule. After reward, backward replay at 160 ms lag carried non-local paths and was stronger for high-utility (gain x need) paths. Forward replay at 30 ms was not.
numbers: N=29. 160 ms backward: non-local t(28)=2.92 p=0.007; higher for high utility t(28)=3.30 p=0.003. 30 ms forward: utility effect t(28)=-0.34 p=0.74. Non-local learning rate 0.70 with 160 ms replay vs 0.61 without (p=0.023). Replay strength vs reward per trial r=0.41 p=0.03.
limits: Correlational; gain not manipulated; small sample; decoding accuracy 47% vs 6% chance; the 160 ms replay is slower than rodent ripple replay and may reflect conscious computation. Forward replay did not show the prioritisation.
agent_relevance: Support that reverse, post-outcome replay is the part that tracks gain x need. Suggests credit-assignment passes after outcomes are where prioritisation pays.

source: Liu, Mattar, Behrens, Daw, Dolan (2020 preprint) Experience replay supports non-local learning
finding: Preprint of the Science paper. Task separates direct from indirect learning. Backward replay after reward was more pronounced for experiences of greater benefit for future behaviour.
numbers: Behaviour: higher learning rate for high-gain paths (0.79 vs 0.37) and high-need paths (0.61 vs 0.54); the difference was significant for gain (p=0.020) but not need (p=0.16). Need levels 17%, 33%, 50% by arm frequency. N=29 (df 28).
limits: Behavioural support is stronger for gain than for need. Need effect on learning rate was not significant on its own.
agent_relevance: Warns that gain may matter more than need in practice; in our agent, estimate gain well before spending effort on need.

source: Schaul, Quan, Antonoglou, Silver (2015) Prioritized Experience Replay
finding: Replay transitions in proportion to TD error (surprise) with importance sampling correction. Beat uniform replay in DQN. Oracle ordering gave exponential speed-ups on a toy task.
numbers: Median normalized score over 49 Atari games 48% (uniform) to 106% (prioritized); better on 41 of 49 games. Over 57 games with the stronger agent, median 111% to 128% and mean 418% to 551%.
limits: Priority uses only error size, not need. Stale priorities for items not replayed. Needs importance-sampling correction to avoid bias.
agent_relevance: The AI ancestor of the idea. TD error is a cheap stand-in for gain; for an LLM loop the analogue is how often a subgoal's check result surprised us.

source: Fedus et al. (2020) Revisiting Fundamentals of Experience Replay
finding: Systematic Atari study. Prioritised replay did not significantly change how well agents used larger replay buffers. Benefit of capacity depended mostly on n-step returns.
numbers: Rainbow without prioritisation still gained +17.3% median when buffer grew 1M to 10M. Without n-step returns, median change -2.3%.
limits: Tested capacity and replay ratio, not a direct head-to-head of PER vs uniform on small buffers. Atari only.
agent_relevance: Failed-to-add result: prioritisation is not a free win. Test ordering against plain uniform or recency before trusting it.

source: Fatemi (2026) Prioritized Replay for RL Post-training
finding: Problem-level priority for LLM RL training: score = p(1-p) where p is the model's success rate on that problem. Mid-difficulty problems get most replay. Fully solved and unsolved problems go to side pools and are retested.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B, GRPO, 1000 GURU math problems, batch 4 problems x 8 rollouts, 250 steps, lr 1e-6, EMA alpha 0.8, 12.5% random exploration batches, retest every 10 steps (1 solved, 3 unsolved). Prioritised almost always above uniform on MATH-500 and AIME 2024 (pass@1 and pass@4). More than 600 of 1000 problems never seen.
limits: Proof of concept, single run, no sweeps, no table of gains. Longer runs plateaued and oscillated. Starvation of unseen problems. Over 60% of problems near-unsolvable for this model.
agent_relevance: p(1-p) is a ready gain proxy for subgoals with pass/fail checks. Keep solved and failed pools and retest them on a schedule to avoid forgetting and starvation.

source: Bae et al. (2025) Online Difficulty Filtering for Reasoning Oriented Reinforcement Learning
finding: Filtering training prompts to those with success rate near 0.5 raises RL convergence speed and final accuracy. Thresholds are set symmetric around success rate 0.5.
numbers: Abstract reports up to +12% gains.
limits: Reasoning-RL training, not inference-time memory. Per-benchmark numbers not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Independent support for the mid-difficulty (gain-like) priority.

source: Jiang et al. (2021) Prioritized Level Replay
finding: Replay training levels by estimated learning potential plus staleness. Improves sample efficiency and generalisation on Procgen.
numbers: Combined with the previous leading method, over 76% improvement in test return relative to standard RL baselines (abstract).
limits: Game levels, not language tasks. Details of the score were not read closely.
agent_relevance: A staleness bonus is the practical analogue of need: items not looked at recently may have changed.

source: Butt, Manczak, Wiggers et al. (2024) CodeIt: Self-Improving Language Models with Prioritized Hindsight Replay
finding: LLM program synthesis on ARC. Hindsight relabelling plus prioritised replay, with priority proportional to the share of demonstration outputs a program matches. Real solutions are replayed more than relabelled ones.
numbers: Solves 59 of 400 ARC eval tasks (about 15%), state of the art at the time. Hindsight relabelling gave about 40% improvement. Ablation A3 uniform sampling: small drop in cumulative performance but large drop in policy performance (forgetting). Shorter program found for 53% of solved tasks in later iterations.
limits: Training-time, needs fine-tuning; ablation reported as plots, three seeds. Priority is outcome match, not gain x need.
agent_relevance: Replaying the best-matching past attempts protected against forgetting. For a scaffold: prioritise stored attempts by partial pass rate.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Possibility and Pass-rate Prioritized Experience Replay (BTP pipeline) for LLM code agents
finding: Stores failed code samples in a buffer with priority P2Value = a x model likelihood + (1-a) x test pass rate; rank-based sampling to fine-tune code models.
numbers: APPS, CodeContests, HumanEval; GPT-2 and GPT-Neo fine-tuned on samples from GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5, CodeLlama-34B, WizardCoder-34B. Self-fine-tuning gains were described as modest but mostly positive.
limits: No clean ablation of prioritised vs uniform replay found in the text read. Code only.
agent_relevance: Failed attempts still carry value when ranked by partial success. Use partial-pass failures as subgoal seeds.

source: Wang, Frans, Abbeel, Levine, Efros (2025) Prioritized Generative Replay, ICLR
finding: Replay buffer replaced by a conditional diffusion model guided by relevance functions such as curiosity or value. Guidance raises diversity and reduces overfitting to rare high-priority samples.
numbers: DMC at 100k steps, 5 seeds; beats REDQ, DrQ-v2 and SynthER on state and pixel tasks. Extra training time under 5% (RL train 2.11 h vs 1.98 h for SynthER, +6.5% in table).
limits: Pure prioritisation overfits as useful samples are rare; generation is used to densify. Continuous control, not language.
agent_relevance: Warns that hard top-priority replay can over-concentrate. Mix in random or varied items.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) MemRL: Self-Evolving Agents via Runtime Reinforcement Learning on Episodic Memory
finding: Frozen LLM, external memory of intent, experience and utility triples. Two-phase retrieval: semantic filter, then rank by learned Q-value utility, updated from reward with a Monte Carlo rule. A direct LLM-agent analogue of utility-ordered memory access.
numbers: Beats best baseline MemP by +3.8% average cumulative success (ALFWorld and OS +6.2% each, HLE +3.6%). Transfer: +2.8% average over MemP. Q-weighting best at 0.5 (inverted U). Q vs success Pearson r=0.861; 21.5% success in lowest Q bin to 88.1% in highest. Retrieval size k1=5,k2=3 beats 3/1 and 10/5. Cross-task vs single-task retrieval: OS +9.0%, ALFWorld +5.1%.
limits: Utility is learned from outcomes (gain-like), no explicit need term. Overhead of Q-tracking not benchmarked. About 12% of memories in the high-Q bin were failures.
agent_relevance: Closest working use of the idea: blend similarity and learned utility about 50:50, learn utility online from outcomes.

source: Cao et al. (2026) Remember Me, Refine Me (ReMe): dynamic procedural memory
finding: Procedural memory with utility-based refinement: counts retrievals and helpfulness, then deletes low-utility items. Experience quality beats quantity.
numbers: BFCL-V3 and AppWorld. Qwen3-8B with ReMe beat larger Qwen3-14B without memory: average +8.83% Avg@4 and +7.29% Pass@4. Retrieval threshold 5 before deletion is considered. Stronger summariser (8B to 32B): Avg@4 +1.83% to +3.33%. Latency 21.42 s to 23.96 s per task.
limits: Deletion effect not isolated from other components in the text read. Tool-use benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Utility-based forgetting is the flip side of prioritised revisit: low-gain items drop out.

source: Authors of arXiv 2505.16067 (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: experience-following and misaligned replay
finding: Agents copy retrieved records: high input similarity gives high output similarity. This causes error propagation and misaligned replay. History-based deletion (remove records retrieved at least n times whose mean utility is below a threshold) can raise performance.
numbers: Four agents: RegAgent, EHRAgent, AgentDriver, CIC-IoT. With no deletion, RegAgent success 70.95 under a strict addition evaluator vs 63.18 under a coarse one. History-based deletion helps with a reliable evaluator but hurt AgentDriver when GPT-4o-mini was the evaluator.
limits: Results table was garbled in text extraction; only a few cells read with confidence. Results depend on evaluator quality.
agent_relevance: Replaying a bad stored subgoal is worse than not replaying. Check stored items against later outcomes; future task results act as free quality labels.

source: Feng et al. (2026) ExpHarness: model-agnostic experience learning through a trainable harness
finding: A trained retrieval copilot sets per task how strongly to favour historically useful experiences over merely similar ones (dial W from 0 to 100), rewarded by the with-vs-without-experience score difference.
numbers: Over strongest baseline: +12.1% and +4.5% on static tasks, +21.4% and +12.7% on agentic tasks (small and large executors); interaction steps cut up to 21.6%. Ablations (five domains): w/o Utility Ranking, w/o Graph Diffusion, Flat Experience, w/o Similarity Filtering all below the full method; Flat Experience dropped most.
limits: Ablations do not isolate utility alone; Flat Experience changes two things at once. Needs RL training of a copilot.
agent_relevance: Supports a task-dependent utility weight: high for familiar task types, low for novel ones.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: interactive simulacra of human behavior
finding: Memory retrieval scores each memory by recency (exponential decay), importance (LLM-rated 1 to 10) and relevance (cosine similarity), each min-max normalised and summed. Reflection fires when summed importance passes a threshold.
numbers: 100 Prolific raters ranked five conditions on believability. TrueSkill: full architecture 29.89 (sigma 0.72); no reflection 26.88; no planning 25.64; no memory, planning or reflection 21.21. Full vs none Cohen's d = 8.16. All Dunn post-hoc p<0.001.
limits: Importance is an LLM guess, not gain x need. Measures believability, not task success. Ablation removes whole components, not scoring weights.
agent_relevance: A cheap three-term priority that works in an LLM loop. Our version could replace importance with gain and recency with need.

source: Moore and Atkeson (1993) Prioritized sweeping; Peng and Williams (1993) Efficient learning and planning within the Dyna framework
finding: Classic AI systems that update states in order of expected change in value, using a queue keyed by size of change. Direct predecessors of Mattar and Daw's gain term.
numbers: Not opened this session; figures not recorded.
limits: Known from citations in papers read; DOI not verified.
agent_relevance: Queue-based update order is cheap: push items whose estimate just changed, pop largest first.

source: Gillespie et al. (2021) Hippocampal replay reflects specific past experiences rather than a plan for subsequent choice, Neuron (from a search summary)
finding: Challenge to a planning role for awake replay: replay content did not reliably predict the next choice in a spatial memory task. The same summary cited Carey 2019 and Igata 2021 as finding no trial-by-trial link between replay content and next trajectory.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Seen only through a search summary; URL is a search link, not the paper.
agent_relevance: Boundary on the theory: replay may serve storage as much as planning. Do not assume need-ordering is how the brain does it.

source: Human hippocampal replay during rest prioritizes weakly learned information and predicts memory performance (search summary)
finding: fMRI in humans: rest-period replay favoured objects that were less well remembered, and more replay predicted better later memory.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Search summary only. Weak-memory priority is gain-like (high where learning is incomplete).
agent_relevance: Supports prioritising poorly consolidated subgoals.

source: Andrychowicz et al. (2017) Hindsight Experience Replay (cited by CodeIt and PPER)
finding: Relabel failed episodes with the goal they actually reached, so failures yield training signal. CodeIt and PPER both use this idea for code.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Known only from citations in papers read.
agent_relevance: Failed subgoal attempts can be stored under what they did achieve.

source: APEX-EM: non-parametric online learning for autonomous agents (arXiv 2603.29093)
finding: Stores full procedural-episodic traces in a graph; retrieves by semantic, structural-signature and graph channels, and indexes successes and failures. Names MemRL as closest prior work.
numbers: Held-out BigCodeBench with shared GPT-4o: +7.6 pp. Lifelong Agent Bench with GPT-4o-mini: +1.4 pp (OS), +1.0 pp (DB). KGQAGen-10k blind 1,079 questions: 73.7% vs 42.0% with no memory. Cites intra-HLE similarity of 0.186 as a regime where embeddings fail.
limits: Same-backbone comparisons; numbers from abstract and intro. No explicit gain or need priority.
agent_relevance: When embedding similarity is weak, structure-based retrieval gives a second route to rank stored items.

source: Trajectory-informed memory generation for self-improving agent systems (arXiv 2603.10600, IBM)
finding: Extracts strategy, recovery and optimisation tips from agent trajectories and injects them by multi-dimensional similarity. Gains are largest on hard tasks.
numbers: AppWorld: up to +14.3 pp scenario goal completion on held-out tasks; +28.5 pp on complex tasks (149% relative).
limits: Retrieval by similarity, not utility; no priority ordering.
agent_relevance: Hard tasks gain most from stored lessons, consistent with gain being larger where the current policy is weak.

source: Search finding: no direct LLM study of the gain x need rule found
finding: Searches of Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the web (arXiv API rate-limited with 429) found no paper that tests gain x need on a language model or names it in an agent loop. Related work uses proxies: p(1-p), TD error, learned Q-utility, importance-recency-relevance.
numbers: About 8 web searches plus several API queries; no count of hits recorded.
limits: Absence of evidence from limited search. 'Successor representation' and 'EVB' not searched separately.
agent_relevance: Using gain x need explicitly would be new. The proxies have measured gains of roughly +3.6 to +12% on benchmarks.

source: Fatemi (2026) failure notes: starvation and plateau
finding: Boundary conditions of problem-level prioritisation: unseen problems starved because known mid-priority ones outranked the default 0.2 prior; 12.5% random exploration did not fix it; larger effective gradients needed a lower learning rate.
numbers: Std of success rates settled near 0.2 in the last 60 steps; no problem reached full success in 250 steps; unsolved pool grew almost linearly.
limits: Author's own observation, no multi-seed check.
agent_relevance: Set the default priority of untried subgoals high enough to be sampled, and reserve a fixed share for exploration.
